title: Conflicting choices: when to balance, choose, limit, or invent "both"
summary: Jason Cohen gives a framework for resolving two conflicting options. Balance only when both extremes are bad, choose when both are rational, choose-to-a-limit when one goal needs a constraint, and invent "both" only with a web of reinforcing decisions that becomes a moat.

principles.text: Seek a balance only when both extremes are bad; it rarely means equal parts.
principles.quote: This is the correct approach when both extremes are bad.

principles.text: When both extremes are rational but contradictory, make a clear choice. A middle path fails to decide.
principles.quote: When the extremes are bad you seek a balance, but when the extremes are both rational choices, it is not a *balance* but rather a _choice_, and choose you must.

principles.text: Pick one customer segment and focus everything on it; don't default to the mid-market as a compromise.
principles.quote: A new startup must [find its Carol--it's ICP--then focus] positioning, marketing, brand, and most of all, product, on that one segment.

principles.text: Claiming 'it's a balance' is often a way to avoid a hard decision.
principles.quote: Often people claim "it's a balance" to justify their refusal to make a decision.

principles.text: Maximize the goal metric while satisficing a constraint, using an objective measure to know when to switch attention.
principles.quote: In this mode, the answer is "Maximize A, while satisficing B." One is the goal, the other is the governor.

principles.text: A 'why not both' strategy needs invention, risk, and a web of other decisions that makes you uncopyable.
principles.quote: Because it requires a network of other self-reinforcing decisions, it creates a unique offering, which remains unique even if competitors copy a subset of your strategy.
